objective: Compare latest institutional positions on AI task productivity, deep firm adoption, aggregate TFP/GDP, distribution, and financing. Not a meta-analysis or probability estimate.
comparability_notes: MIT FutureTech 11% deeply integrated S&P 500 and NBER 78% any-use cross-country are not contradictory: population and adoption-stage definitions differ.
MIT task coding +180% and shipped software +30% show throughput bottlenecks, not necessarily revenue or GDP impacts.

Acemoglu <0.53% ten-year cumulative TFP-level estimate, IMF +0.5pp/year global growth potential, NBER 3.6% GDP level implied by equity markets and BIS 5.5% conditional long-run growth are different units/models/horizons.
ECB saved time is survey-reported opportunity, not verified real output; self-report estimates cannot be substituted for national accounts.
2025/2026 studies include present and prospective expectations; all should be tied to their measurement windows.
Informal institutional blog summaries and official speeches do not equal original paper methodological review.

institutions.institution: MIT FutureTech / Initiative on the Digital Economy
institutions.method: LLM-coded self-disclosure in annual SEC Form 10-K filings; firms in S&P 500; 2016–2025
institutions.finding: 11% deeply integrated AI at 2025 year-end, further 10% AI in production of goods/services; no measured difference in output per employee versus non-adopters; exploratory correlations and company reporting do not identify treatment effects
institutions.caveat: SEC disclosure is not independent operational audit. Only large US listed firms; lag between filings and deployment.

institutions.publication: Writing Code vs. Shipping Code — Productivity Effects Across Generations of Coding Tools
institutions.method: Reported MIT Sloan summary of observational GitHub data for >100,000 developers across coding-to-release stages
institutions.finding: Up to 180% more coding activity under combined coding-tool usage; 50% more projects and 30% more releases; no corresponding app-download/review gains. These are different units and not a controlled GDP effect.

metrics.unit: percent relative increase, maximum cumulative coding activity
metrics.name: coding activity

institutions.caveat: Original full working paper not independently audited in this pass; matching/selection and quality of shipped code need checking.

institutions.method: Task-based general-equilibrium model, assumptions on automatable tasks and task savings
institutions.finding: Published model estimates a total factor productivity level gain below 0.53% over ten years (upper bound 0.66% before hard-task adjustment); NOT +0.53 percentage points of annual growth.

metrics.unit: percent cumulative TFP level gain (upper bound)
metrics.period: next ten years from model baseline
metrics.name: adjusted TFP projection

institutions.caveat: 2024 MIT landing page still shows superseded 0.55%/0.71% draft estimates. Use 2025 accepted manuscript for version-consistent comparison.

institutions.method: Conceptual task taxonomy and examples, not empirical country-level effect estimate
institutions.finding: Automation/capital augmentation may raise productivity without boosting worker income; new human-task creation is classified as unambiguously pro-worker.
institutions.caveat: Normative claim about direction of technology; not a measured distributional response.

institutions.publication: The Macroeconomic Effect of AI: Sizing the Software Engineering Channel
institutions.method: Infer AI software-engineering productivity gains from firm equity return sensitivity to AI factor and software engineer payroll share, then pass through structural macro model
institutions.finding: Market-implied software engineering productivity equivalent +32.6% permanent (Nov 2022–Dec 2025), model translates to +3.6% level of GDP baseline or +6.5% with R&D channel; these are investor-expectation/model outputs, not observed 2026 GDP.
institutions.caveat: Forward-looking asset-pricing assumptions, identification of AI factor and valuation changes could bias inferred effect; not directly comparable with Acemoglu TFP.

institutions.publication: Canaries in the Gold Mine: Early Productivity Gains from Artificial Intelligence Creating Organization Capital
institutions.method: Firm AI-skilled employment and job-description proxy for organizational capital; firm-level associations
institutions.finding: Recent AI-skilled hiring is associated with productivity growth through organizational capital in recent years, not in earlier decade; mechanism is hypothesis based on firm data.
institutions.caveat: AI-skilled employment is a proxy for AI investment; unobserved management quality or selection could explain correlations.

institutions.method: Summer 2026 responses from nearly 9,000 senior executives in 7 countries
institutions.finding: 78% of sampled firms use AI; average past self-attributed productivity-growth increment 0.2% per year; expected 0.6% per year in next 3 years. These are executive retrospective and forward-looking reports.

metrics.unit: percent per year additional labor productivity growth (self-attributed)
metrics.name: subjective retrospective effect

metrics.unit: percent per year expected additional labor productivity growth
metrics.name: subjective expectation

institutions.caveat: Not equivalent to 11% deep integration in S&P 500; any use versus organizational integration, different frames, biased self-reports.

institutions.method: Official cross-national productivity compilation and literature synthesis
institutions.finding: Task gains have not been cleanly detected as broad AI-caused aggregate productivity yet; organizational adaptation/J-curve is a candidate explanation, not a guarantee.
institutions.caveat: Current national data are affected by macroeconomic and measurement confounders; descriptive macro series do not identify AI-only effects.

institutions.publication: The State of AI 2026: On the Road to ROI
institutions.method: Online survey of 1,719 respondents across 97 nations, fielded 2026-05-04 to 2026-06-08; country-GDP response-weighted
institutions.finding: 80% respondents report own productivity gains; 37% attribute any enterprise EBIT impact to AI; ~6% meet self-reported high-performer definition. Nearly 75% high performers report workflow redesign vs 25% of other respondents.
institutions.caveat: Self-reported impact; highly selective high performers and endogenous redesign; not a causal experiment.

institutions.method: Euro area ECB SAFE/CTS/CES and EU Commission survey comparisons
institutions.finding: Among European midcaps/SMEs in EU Commission Q1 2026 survey, 42% use AI/automation: 30% limited/experimental and 12% extensive. In ECB SAFE Q4 2025, only 7% report significant AI use. European workers surveyed: 52% any job use in 2026.
institutions.caveat: Different samples and questions; 42%, 7% and 52% are not comparable as a homogeneous time series.

institutions.publication: AI adoption and the productivity promise: what workers report
institutions.method: ECB monthly CES about 20k adults from 11 euro-area countries; self-reported AI use/time saved
institutions.finding: Work AI use 52% of respondent workers in 2026 versus 26% in 2024, implied aggregate work-time savings ~3.8% per ECB computation; this is not measured realized GDP or TFP.

metrics.unit: percent total working time saved (perceived, aggregate)
metrics.name: reported time savings

institutions.caveat: Saved time can be idle/reallocated; no proof extra output. Several comparisons of weekly hours saved involve different denominators.

institutions.publication: The World Can't Afford to Get AI Wrong
institutions.method: Policy article explaining scenarios, IMF research and external investment inputs
institutions.finding: Potential growth boost around 0.5 percentage points per year worldwide over the next decade (conditional); current investment/demand shock comes before verified economy-wide productivity/supply shock.

metrics.unit: percentage points additional annual global growth, approximate scenario
metrics.name: potential annual growth effect

institutions.caveat: Not a measured realized productivity gain; distinguish GDP growth from TFP or level GDP.

institutions.method: Endogenous growth calibrated model with innovation tied to rents from consumer goods
institutions.finding: Automation may depress consumption share/demand and innovation incentives; calibrated demand-bottleneck scenario can slow growth below assumed pre-AI 2% after temporary lift; transformative scenario reaches 5.5% after two decades.
institutions.caveat: Scenario output not a historical observation or BIS central forecast; conditional assumptions produce radically different paths.

institutions.publication: Artificial Intelligence in UK Financial Services 2026
institutions.method: Regulatory survey, 196 UK financial firms (105 full surveys); cross-survey comparability guarded
institutions.finding: 86% respondent firms use AI; only 2% of firms report AI agents with broad autonomy; integration 23% and legacy systems 22% are large non-regulatory adoption constraints among question respondents.
institutions.caveat: Sector respondents are not all UK firms; figures based on differing full/short question groups; 2024 sample/question scope differs.

editorial_blocks: Check underlying MIT Demirer/Musolff/Yang original paper, causal identification and release definition.
Check NBER 2026 market-implied growth model assumptions before aggregating scenarios.
Confirm ECB speech exact financial data definitions and NBER full revision metadata.
Source licensing and re-use review; data stored as source links and independent short paraphrases.
No release to public case registry or HTML before human review.
